gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the '0.2-second' trigger and 12-month battery claims are photo-mode figures. In TrailCamPro's tests the Bushnell Core S-4K started recording video in 0.70 s and its batteries lasted 2.4 months on video, while the Browning Dark Ops Pro X 1080 started video in 0.3 s.
standout_why: I opened Outdoor Life's best trail cameras 2026 page and TechGearLab's best trail camera page. TechGearLab gives one advertised trigger speed per camera ('0.2 sec' for the Bushnell Core S-4K) and never separates photo from video. It gives no battery-life figure for any camera. It does flag interpolated megapixels for the GardePro A3S. Outdoor Life covers neither the Bushnell nor the Browning, gives no photo-vs-video trigger figures and says it does not explain interpolated megapixels. The Wirecutter proxy URL returned HTTP 403, so I could not check it. ChatGPT's answer repeats the photo-mode claims ('Fast 0.2-second photo trigger', 'specified 0.22-second trigger') and sets 0.3 s or faster as its target. It never says that video mode, which many motion-activated buyers use, is much slower on the Bushnell.
decides: For photos, the Bushnell Core S-4K is still the fastest: TrailCamPro measured 0.08 s against 0.19 s for the Browning. If the shopper wants video, the pick flips. The Browning Dark Ops Pro X 1080 starts video in 0.3 s against the Bushnell's 0.70 s. It also detected motion farther (90 ft at a 46.8° detection angle, against 70 ft at 33.6°) and lasted slightly longer on video batteries (2.6 against 2.4 months). Both makers' battery claims only hold for photos: in video mode the batteries lasted roughly 1/9 to 1/10 as long. On the page, the table should show photo trigger, video trigger, photo battery and video battery side by side. The footnote should say that the advertised numbers are photo-mode numbers.
